section.title: Python Exceptions in Rexx
section.para: A Python exception raised by a call from Rexx is the condition SYNTAX 98.900, whose message is Python error: followed by the exception's type and text: Python error: TypeError: .... Its condition object has, in the ADDITIONAL Array:

listitem.para: the traceback, as Python formats it (an empty string for an exception raised with , which has none yet).

section.para: This is the layout of BSF4ooRexx, whose additional[2] is the Java exception.
Rexx code traps it as any SYNTAX condition: with a catch clause, the preferred way, or the legacy way, signal on syntax or call on syntax.

example.title: A Python exception, trapped in Rexx
example.programlisting:
do say .py~int("seven") catch c = syntax say c~code say c~message e = c~additional[2] -- the exception say .py~type(e)~getattr("__name__") e~args end
::requires "python.cls"
example.screen: 98.900 Python error: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'seven'. ValueError ("invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'seven'",)

section.title: Raising Python Exceptions from Rexx
section.para: raises a Python exception from Rexx code: an exception object, or an exception class called with the remaining arguments. In Rexx it is the same SYNTAX 98.900 as when Python raises it.

example.title: .py~raise
example.programlisting:
do .py~raise(.py~KeyError, "missing") catch c = syntax say c~message say .py~isinstance(c~additional[2], .py~KeyError) end
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: Exceptions that Go Back to Python
section.para: A Python exception that goes through Rexx code back to Python is raised again as itself. Python calls Rexx (a callback, an override of a class that extends a Python class, a routine), the Rexx code calls Python, which raises; if the Rexx code does not trap the condition, the Python caller gets the original exception, with its traceback. Python's protocols depend on it: a sequence ends with IndexError, an iterator with StopIteration, a mapping says "missing" with KeyError.

The other way round, a Rexx condition that goes through Python back to Rexx is raised again as itself. Rexx calls Python (a function, an ADDRESS environment written in Python), Python calls Rexx code that fails, and if Python does not catch the , the Rexx caller gets the original condition, not SYNTAX 98.900: a SYNTAX error with its code and message, any other condition with its description, ADDITIONAL and result (a SYNTAX error raised with raise syntax ... description keeps its description). This holds for any condition the Rexx code raises and does not trap: USER, NOTREADY, ERROR, FAILURE, LOSTDIGITS and the rest reach Python as a RexxError that Python can catch, and, if it does not, go back to the Rexx caller, where a CATCH clause, SIGNAL ON or CALL ON traps them as if no Python were in between, an ERROR or FAILURE with its RC. When the Rexx code raised the condition with raise ... return value, the caller gets that value, as in plain Rexx, and the condition object's RESULT is that value too.

A HALT is SYNTAX 4.1 by the time it leaves that Rexx code (Python sees Rexx error 4.1), and back in Rexx it is a HALT again, as if the Rexx code had raised it with no Python in between: a CATCH HALT clause or SIGNAL ON HALT traps it, CALL ON HALT runs its handler and the clause resumes with the call giving .nil, and a caller that does not trap HALT gets SYNTAX 4.1. Its description, ADDITIONAL and result are lost on the way: ooRexx drops them when it turns the HALT into 4.1, so the call gives .nil even when the Rexx code raised the HALT with raise halt ... return value.

Through an ADDRESS environment written in Python, which is a command handler like those written in Rexx (), a condition goes back as from a handler written in Rexx: SYNTAX as itself, any other condition with its description and ADDITIONAL, its result, if it has one, as the command's RC. A HALT is a HALT again there too: a CATCH HALT clause or SIGNAL ON HALT traps it, CALL ON HALT resumes the command with RC 0, and untrapped it ends as SYNTAX 4.1.

section.title: Thrown Conditions
section.para: ooRexx's THROW instruction throws a condition: unlike one raised with RAISE, which goes one level, it goes from caller to caller until something catches it, whatever its name, as a SYNTAX error does (ooRexx Reference, Thrown Conditions; the instruction is experimental in ooRexx). Python in between changes nothing. Rexx code that Python called throws a condition: if the Python code does not catch it (it is an whose thrown is &True;), it goes on in the Rexx code that called Python, and from there to its callers. A CATCH clause or SIGNAL ON catches it on any of those levels; CALL ON does not trap it, as it does not trap a SYNTAX error; the FINALLY clauses of the levels it leaves run; and a condition that nothing catches ends the program with error 4.1, or 4.901, which shows its description. Its condition object says THROWN .true, and keeps its description and ADDITIONAL.

Python code throws a Rexx condition with : oorexx.throw("user badConfig", description="...") is Rexx's throw user badConfig description "...", thrown in the Rexx code that called Python. It is the counterpart of , with which Rexx code raises a Python exception.

example.title: Thrown conditions, through Python and from Python
example.programlisting:
do say total(.array~of("pear", "fig")) say total(.array~of("pear", "kiwi")) catch c = user noPrice say c~condition":" c~description "(thrown:" c~thrown")" end
.py~exec("import oorexx" || "0a"x || - "def port(config):" || "0a"x || - " if 'port' not in config:" || "0a"x || - " oorexx.throw('user badConfig', description='no port', additional=[config])" || "0a"x || - " return config['port']") do say .py~main~port(.py~dict(.py~kw("port", 8080))) say .py~main~port(.py~dict~new) catch c = user badConfig say c~condition":" c~description c~additional[1] end
::routine total -- does not catch it: it goes on use arg basket return .py~sum(.py~map(.context~package~findRoutine("PRICE"), basket)) ::routine price -- called by Python's map use arg item if item == "pear" then return 3 if item == "fig" then return 2 throw user noPrice description ("no price for" item) ::requires "python.cls"
example.screen: 5 USER NOPRICE: no price for kiwi (thrown: 1) 8080 USER BADCONFIG: no port {}

section.para: Through an ADDRESS environment written in Python, a thrown condition goes on as through a handler written in Rexx: thrown, to the code that issued the command and to its callers, an ERROR or a FAILURE with its RC.

section.title: Rexx Conditions in Python
section.para: Any other Rexx condition that reaches Python, an error in Rexx code that Python called, is an , whose text is Rexx's message: Rexx error 42.3: Arithmetic overflow; divisor must not be zero. A condition that is not an error has its name and, if it has one, its description: Rexx condition USER BADCONFIG: no port. Its attributes are the parts of the condition: its code, its line, its program, its texts, its traceback, and whether it was thrown ().

example.title: Rexx errors and Python exceptions, seen from Python
example.screen: RexxError True Rexx error 42.3: Arithmetic overflow; divisor must not be zero. KeyError 'nope'
